question.text: The Atlanta Compromise was criticized as weak by W.E.B. Du Bois and other co-founders of this American civil rights organization. Thurgood Marshall represented this group in arguments before the Supreme Court, including Brown v. Board.
question.answerHtml: NAACP (accept National Association for the Advancement of Colored People)
question.clue: Ralph David Abernathy was first part of this group before he led the SCLC.

swap.text: This word describes the illegal production and sale of liquor during Prohibition. It also applies to anything taken without permission and distributed for profit.
swap.clue: The Purple Gang in Detroit had a major influence on this industry, which imported its main product from Belle Isle and Windsor.

question.text: The Italian-American Mafia rose to prominence by selling bootleg alcohol following the passage of this policy, which outlawed the consumption and sale of alcohol.
question.clue: Wayne Wheeler drafted a bill that would enforce this policy.

swap.leadin: A letter written to this man in 1934 proclaims "Even if my business hasn't been strictly legal, it don't hurt anything to tell you what a fine car you got in the V-8."
swap.text: Name this American industrialist whose company introduced its first V-8 car in 1932, five years after it discontinued its landmark Model T.
swap.clue: This businessman used the scientific management ideas of Frederick W. Taylor to improve efficiency on each of the eighty-four steps of his signature product.

question.text: This woman recruited many women to the Knights of Labor. She later led the Children's Crusade and was a founding member of the IWW.
question.clue: To protest the use of child labor in Pennsylvania silk mills, this activist marched young mill workers 120 miles to the house of Teddy Roosevelt.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Native American policy in the Roaring Twenties.
swap.text: The Snyder Act, which granted Indians U.S. citizenship, was signed into law by this president. This Republican president succeeded Warren G. Harding.
swap.clue: He clashed with the American Federation of Labor to put down the Boston Police Strike.

question.leadin: Mass withdrawals of money from trusts during this event led to the creation of the Federal Reserve.
question.text: Name this financial crisis caused by the failure of the Knickerbocker Trust Company.
question.clue: This crisis occurred after an attempt by Otto and Augustus Heinze to corner the United Copper Company.

swap.leadin: This journalist used her contact with Henry H. Rogers to write investigative pieces for McClure's magazine which she later compiled into a book.
swap.text: Name this woman who described J.D Rockefeller's manipulation of railroad rates in The History of the Standard Oil Company.
swap.clue: In 1904, this muckraking journalist wrote The History of Standard Oil Company, detailing the company's abusive practices as part of a series of articles for McClure's Magazine.

question.leadin: Examples include the construction of Hukuang Railroad and the refinancing of national debt in Haiti and Honduras.
question.text: Name this William Howard Taft foreign policy that attempted to substitute investment for military force.
question.clue: This policy aided in the overthrow of Jose Santos Zelaya and the installment of Adolfo Diaz in order to guarantee loans to the Nicaraguan government.

swap.leadin: William Monroe Trotter went to Paris to campaign for an expansion to these proposals that addressed racial equality.
swap.text: Identify this set of proposals that included a restoration of all territory to Belgium and the creation of an independent Polish state.
swap.clue: This speech advocated the elimination of secret treaties, colonial adjustment, and reduction in arms.

question.text: This president supported the Hepburn Act, and added a namesake corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. Earlier, he served as New York governor, and lieutenant colonel of the Rough Riders.
question.clue: This author of biographies of Thomas Hart Benton and Oliver Cromwell also collected speeches and essays in a book titled for one of his principles, The Strenuous Life.

swap.text: Eugene Debs was arrested under this law, passed in 1917 and strengthened by the Sedition Act of 1918, which criminalized most opposition to World War I.
swap.clue: Goldman was prosecuted under this law, which was passed during World War I and later used against Edward Snowden. It was upheld in Schenck v. U.S., establishing the "clear and present danger" test.

question.leadin: Several of these cases arose from disputes over applying customs duties and tariffs to goods at the Port of New York.
question.text: Name this series of 1901 Supreme Court cases, which metaphorically answered whether the Constitution follows the flag, finding the Constitution does not necessarily apply to territories.
question.clue: This 1901 set of Supreme Court cases. These cases prevented newly-acquired U.S. territories from being incorporated into the Union based on the difficulty of enacting "Anglo-Saxon principles."

swap.leadin: Apologies to our American friends, but, answer some questions about hypocrisy in American history.
swap.text: This event of 1919 killed 21 and injured 150 people, more than four times as many fatalities as the Boston massacre in the same city.
swap.answerHtml: The Great Molasses Flood (accept Boston Molasses Flood, accept Molasses Disaster)
swap.clue: This event in which 21 people died after a tank belonging to the Purity Distilling Company exploded in Boston's North End.

question.text: The Dodge brothers got their start manufacturing transmissions for this man's namesake company. This man patented the stationary assembly line to mass-produce the Curved Dash.

swap.leadin: A split arose between this movement and preservationism, which did not advocate the use of national lands for industry as well as for setting them aside for their natural beauty.
swap.text: Name this movement, one of whose members was George Perkins Marsh, a precursor of environmentalism that saw success with the establishment of Yellowstone National Park.
swap.clue: A program named for this cause was headed by Robert Fechner and employed young men in tent camps.

question.text: While on the court of appeals, Parker wrote the majority opinion in a ruling which found against this man and claimed that the state of New York had "beyond question" an interest in clean bakeries; that ruling was reversed by the Supreme Court in 1905.

swap.leadin: The Associated Press sued this magazine for libel after the printing of a cartoon depicting the news giant "Poisoned at the Source."
swap.text: Name this socialist magazine that was shut down in 1917 over its editors' anti-war stances. Jack Reed covered the trial of "Big Bill" Haywood and other Wobblies for this graphic magazine.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about American propaganda.
question.text: The World War I agency called the Committee on Public Information was also named for this chairman, a journalist who wrote the book How We Advertised America. His agency tried to persuade Americans as to the righteousness of the war's cause.
question.clue: This one-time head of the Committee on Public Information.

swap.leadin: Name these figures associated with the Republic of Texas FTPE.
swap.text: This native Kentuckian served as aide-de-camp to Sam Houston during the war of independence, and then was named Texas's Secretary of War by Mirabeau Lamar. The leader of Confederate forces in the West, he was killed at the battle of Shiloh.
swap.clue: This congressman used the data of the 1890 census to set the quotas for new immigrants in the Immigrant Act of 1924, which he co-sponsored and names with Senator David Reed.
